name: Garnet
workload: RESP-translated YCSB-A workload, 256M 8-byte keys, string values 8B-several KB, using memtier_benchmark and Garnet's own Resp.bench load generator against Garnet/Valkey/KeyDB/Dragonfly on Azure Standard F72s_v2 VMs (72 vCPUs, 144GB RAM), Ubuntu 24.04, accelerated TCP networking
claimed_speedup: Table 1 (normalized to Redis): node throughput 108x, P99 latency at batch size 16 down to 0.25x; memtier GET throughput >=20x higher and P99 latency 3x lower than Valkey at high client load; up to 40x/6x higher throughput than KeyDB/Dragonfly in some GET experiments; checkpoint speed 257x, scale-out (migration) speed 94x vs Redis
hardware: Azure Standard F72s_v2 VMs, 72 vCPUs, 144GB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04 with accelerated TCP networking
stars_or_usage: 12k stars; described as widely deployed inside Microsoft
tradeoffs: Runs on the .NET runtime (GC, JIT) rather than being a native binary; kernel-bypass networking (eRPC/DPDK path) used for the best latency numbers is a prototype not shipped in the open-source build; complex RESP data types (SortedSet, HyperLogLog) add overhead
caveats: Evaluation performed and published by Garnet's own authors (Microsoft Research + Facebook/Meta-adjacent academics via VLDB peer review), not a fully independent third party, though it is peer-reviewed (PVLDB 19(2):224-237) with full hardware/workload disclosure; memtier_benchmark itself became client-bottlenecked at high throughput so most headline figures use Garnet's own Resp.bench tool instead
found_via: GitHub: microsoft/FASTER README (deprecated, points to Garnet as successor) -> gh api repos/microsoft/garnet; VLDB paper fetched via WebFetch from https://badrish.net/papers/garnet-vldb2026.pdf and read as PDF

name: go-sieve
workload: Go benchmark suite (bench/) comparing SIEVE vs hashicorp/golang-lru v2.0.7 (LRU and ARC): parallel Get/Add/Probe/Delete/Mixed micro-benchmarks, Zipfian-distribution read benchmarks, core-scaling sweep (1-10 GOMAXPROCS), and real-world trace replay (MSR Cambridge, Meta Storage, ~300M requests) for hit-ratio and memory.
claimed_speedup: "13-55x faster than hashicorp/golang-lru per trace on real-world cache traces (warm cache, 10 cores)"; under cold-cache mixed read/write replay "2-6x faster". Micro-benchmark table: Get_Parallel 5.76 ns/op (Sieve) vs 144.2 ns/op (LRU) vs 144.9 ns/op (ARC); at GOMAXPROCS=10, Get_Parallel is 14.9->5.5 ns/op for Sieve while LRU degrades from 31.4 to 121.1 ns/op with added cores.
compiler_and_flags: go1.26.3, GOMAXPROCS=10, `go test -bench` (commands in bench/Makefile: make bench / make trace / make sweep)
hardware: Apple M4, 10 cores (4 performance + 6 efficiency), macOS Darwin 25.5.0, arm64
tradeoffs: Lock-free reads only work with the columnar slot-state design (extra bookkeeping array); Delete_Parallel is the one micro-benchmark where SIEVE loses to LRU's simpler single-lock unlink (81.2 vs 69.5 ns/op); at extreme Zipf skew (s=1.50) SIEVE's advantage narrows to ~6%.
caveats: Benchmarked on a single machine (Apple M4) by the repo author; no independent/third-party confirmation. Very new/low-star project (41 stars) but methodology, raw results file, and reproduction commands are all public, meeting tier A requirements (code + compiler + CPU all stated).
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "SIEVE" "cache" --sort stars

name: otter
workload: Go port of the Caffeine JMH GetPutBenchmark: 8 goroutines against a pre-populated, max-size-bounded cache under a Zipf access distribution, at read/write ratios of 100/0, 75/25, 50/50, 25/75 and 0/100, comparing otter, theine, ristretto, sturdyc, ccache, gcache, ttlcache and golang-lru.
claimed_speedup: At reads=100%,writes=0%: otter 106,390,749 ops/s (9.399 ns/op) vs golang-lru 3,138,739 ops/s (318.6 ns/op) — about 34x higher throughput (derived from page data). At reads=75%,writes=25%: otter 78,478,946 ops/s vs golang-lru not in that excerpt but ristretto/theine trail otter by ~1.2-3x.
compiler_and_flags: go 1.24.0 (per go.mod), `go test -bench` default flags
hardware: Apple M1 Pro, goos=darwin, goarch=arm64
stars_or_usage: 2.7k stars; used in Grafana, Centrifugo, FrankenPHP, Unkey, Nuclei
tradeoffs: Otter's sophisticated TinyLFU-based admission/eviction policy costs more per-eviction CPU time than simple mutex-protected LRU under 100%-insert/eviction-heavy workloads — the project's own eviction benchmark shows golang-lru (266-461 ns/op) beating otter (307-417 ns/op) in that specific worst-case scenario, even though otter wins decisively on read-heavy throughput.
caveats: Read-throughput comparison numbers come from a raw `go test -bench` text file in the repo (tier A: code, compiler version via go.mod, and CPU model all present); note the same project's eviction-only benchmark shows the opposite ranking for pure-insert workloads, so the 'faster than LRU' claim is workload-dependent (read-heavy, not eviction-heavy).
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "W-TinyLFU" --sort stars

name: AdaptSize
baseline: LRU (via unmodified Varnish Cache, a concurrent-LRU CDN memory cache with no admission control)
workload: Production CDN edge-cache trace replay comparing an unmodified Varnish Cache deployment against Varnish patched with the AdaptSize size-and-popularity-aware admission policy
claimed_speedup: AdaptSize achieves a 0.66 hit ratio vs 0.42 for unmodified Varnish (1.57x improvement), and stabilizes hit ratio variability (coefficient of variation 5% vs 23%, a 4.6x improvement), with no added throughput overhead (scales identically to unmodified Varnish)
compiler_and_flags: gcc 4.4.7 (specific optimization flags not stated)
hardware: FUJITSU CX250 HPC servers, dual Intel Xeon E5-2670 CPUs, 32GB RAM, RHEL 6.5 / kernel 2.6.32, IB QDR networking
tradeoffs: Proof-of-concept quality, not production-ready per its own README; admission-only policy (still relies on Varnish's own LRU eviction); needs periodic re-solving of its size-to-admission-probability model
caveats: Compiler version is stated (gcc 4.4.7) but exact optimization flags are not, so capped at tier B rather than A; production-trace comparison is against Varnish specifically, not raw textbook LRU or memcached/Redis
found_via: gh api users/dasebe/repos; gh api repos/dasebe/AdaptSize/readme; NSDI'17 paper PDF

name: cachegrand
workload: memtier_benchmark GET requests against the Redis-protocol interface, 128-byte values, 25 clients/node across 2 load-generation nodes (config 'd128-c25'), server run with varying worker-thread counts (t1-t64); Redis v7.0.11 vs cachegrand v0.2.1, 3 runs averaged
claimed_speedup: At the 't16' server config, cachegrand reaches 935,576.61 ops/sec (AGGREGATED AVERAGE, 3 runs) on GET vs Redis v7.0.11's 71,143.97 ops/sec (its only reported config, since Redis is single-threaded) - approx 13.2x (derived from page data). At matched single-thread (t1), cachegrand is only ~1.1x faster (78,840.39 vs 71,143.97 ops/sec) (derived from page data); repo README states it 'can handle millions of operations per second' and scales ~linearly with added CPUs
hardware: AMD EPYC 7502P (32c/64t), 8x32GB DDR4-3200 RAM, Ubuntu 22.04 (kernel 5.15), 2x25Gbit Intel XXV710 NICs; identical hardware used for the Redis and cachegrand runs (per cachegrand-benchmarks/benchmarks/cachegrand/v0.2.1/d128-c25/README.md)
tradeoffs: Only implements a subset of the Redis protocol/command set (still WIP per README); multi-threaded architecture means the 13x figure mostly reflects Redis's single-threaded design rather than a faster per-operation algorithm (per-thread parity is closer to ~1.1x); Linux x86-64/aarch64 only; project is a young, self-published key-value store, not a drop-in Memcached/Redis replacement (Memcached protocol support listed as 'planned', not implemented)
caveats: Raw benchmark data and scripts are public (cachegrand-benchmarks repo) and hardware/CPU model are fully documented, but the compiler and build flags used to produce the tested binaries/Docker images are not stated anywhere in the benchmark repo, capping this at tier B rather than A; last commit to the main cachegrand repo is from 2025-01-02 (project appears currently inactive); benchmarks are self-published by the project author, not independently reproduced
found_via: gh search repos "cachegrand" (surfaced while searching registries/GitHub for 'concurrent cache library fast' beating Redis); cachegrand is not itself listed in vcpkg/conan/crates.io/pkg.go.dev/PyPI, included as a Package-registries-adjacent GitHub find

name: CacheLib
workload: CacheBench synthetic look-aside cache workload (Facebook's application look-aside pattern): 100 million objects, cache sizes 8-144GB, 32 threads each, both systems configured with LRU eviction; small caches stress eviction (set-heavy), large caches stress LRU-head updates (get-heavy)
claimed_speedup: "Across all cache sizes, CacheLib achieves higher throughputs than Memcached, processing up to 60% more requests per second than Memcached" (hit ratios similar, Memcached slightly higher at small sizes, CacheLib higher at large sizes)
stars_or_usage: 1.6k stars; used to power look-aside, CDN, and flash caches at Facebook (replacing internal Memcached deployments)
tradeoffs: Embedded in-process C++ library, not a standalone network server like Memcached (must be linked into the application or wrapped in one); larger API surface (DRAM+flash hybrid tiers, pools, warm restart); higher throughput attributed to reduced lock contention (flat combining on the LRU list head) rather than a fundamentally different algorithm
caveats: Benchmark is from the CacheLib design paper written by its own authors (Berg et al., OSDI 2020), comparing against 'a minimally changed Memcached v1.6.6'; CacheBench (the benchmarking harness used) is public in the CacheLib repo, but the paper's evaluation section does not state the CPU model or compiler/build flags used for this specific experiment, so it falls short of tier A; no independent third-party reproduction found
found_via: vcpkg registry (ports/cachelib port exists in microsoft/vcpkg) cross-checked with gh search repos "cachelib"; benchmark sourced from the CacheLib OSDI'20 paper PDF (curl + pdftotext) linked from its USENIX page

name: Cacheus
workload: 17,766 simulation experiments over FIU, MSR and CloudPhysics block-storage traces at varying cache sizes, comparing hit rate against ARC, LIRS, DLIRS and LeCaR
claimed_speedup: Cacheus (using SR-LRU + CR-LFU experts) is statistically significantly better than ARC/LIRS/DLIRS/LeCaR in the majority of paired t-tests across 17,766 experiments; best-case improvement of 38.32% higher hit rate than ARC (CloudPhysics trace, 10% cache size); worst case is a 15.12% hit-rate degradation vs DLIRS (MSR trace, 5% cache size)
license: reference (no LICENSE file found in repo)
tradeoffs: Not uniformly better than every competitor (worst case is a real hit-rate loss vs DLIRS); adaptive combination of multiple experts (ARC/LIRS/LFU-style) adds bookkeeping overhead vs plain LRU; reference Python implementation is a research prototype, not built for production throughput (a C port exists inside libCacheSim)
caveats: Pure trace-driven simulation, no throughput/latency numbers or hardware given; repo has no OSI license file so treated as reference-only for reuse
found_via: gh search repos 'cacheus'; FAST'21 paper PDF (usenix.org)

name: Caffeine
workload: JMH microbenchmark (ComputeBenchmark/GetPutBenchmark) at 16 threads, varying read/write mixes (100% read, 75/25 read/write, 100% write) on a bounded in-process cache, vs ConcurrentLinkedHashMap, Guava Cache, Ehcache, Infinispan and plain ConcurrentHashMap
claimed_speedup: server-class (Xeon E5-2698B v3, 16 threads): 100% read 382.4M ops/s vs 313.9M (ConcurrentLinkedHashMap, ~1.2x) and 43.1M (Guava, ~8.9x); 75/25 read/write 279.4M vs 122.3M (~2.3x) and 37.3M (Guava, ~7.5x); 100% write 48.3M vs 39.8M (~1.2x)
hardware: Server-class: single-socket Xeon E5-2698B v3 @ 2.00GHz, 16 cores (hyperthreading disabled), 224GB RAM, Ubuntu 15.04, Azure G4 instance; desktop-class: MacBook Pro i7-4870HQ @ 2.50GHz
stars_or_usage: 17.9k stars; used as the cache implementation inside Spring, Cassandra, Solr and others
tradeoffs: In-process JVM cache, not a distributed/remote cache like Redis or Memcached, so it solves a different deployment problem (per-process hit ratio and speed rather than shared/networked state); W-TinyLFU admission policy adds bookkeeping vs a plain LRU
caveats: CPU model and OS are stated but the exact JVM version/flags used for the JMH run are not given in the wiki page as fetched; benchmark code and harness are public in the repo (ComputeBenchmark.java, GetPutBenchmark.java) which is why this is scored B rather than C
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos --topic cache --language c++ did not surface this; found via reasoning about 'LRU baselines the benchmark names' + gh api repos/ben-manes/caffeine, then WebFetch of the Benchmarks wiki page

name: GL-Cache
workload: Production CDN/KV traces replayed through a Memcached-like prototype on CloudLab, measuring both hit ratio and throughput; group-level (not per-object) learned eviction
claimed_speedup: GL-Cache achieves 64% higher throughput than LRB (the prior object-level learned cache) at similar hit ratio; paper's evaluation table also reports GL-Cache beating LRU and size-aware Belady baselines directly, though the exact LRU-relative percentage is not isolated in the text we extracted
hardware: CloudLab Utah site m510 nodes: Intel Xeon D-1548 and Intel Xeon Gold 6142, 384GB DRAM
tradeoffs: Batches evictions over object groups instead of single objects, trading some eviction precision for far lower learning/inference overhead than object-level learned caches (e.g. LRB)
caveats: The clearest quantified comparison in the extracted text is against LRB, not literally against raw LRU/memcached; less exercised code path than the core libCacheSim algorithms (opt-in build flag)
found_via: junchengyang.com publication page; libCacheSim README algorithm list

name: Hyperbolic Caching
workload: Django-Wiki and NodeJS web applications using a modified Redis (forked at 3.0) as a look-aside cache, replaying Wikipedia (Jan 2008) and synthetic cost-aware workloads; also Memcachier-style trace-driven miss-rate simulation
claimed_speedup: Hyperbolic caching (random-sampling-based priority eviction) improves end-to-end application throughput by ~5-10% over default Redis while also lowering miss rate; e.g. NodeJS-over-Redis benchmark: throughput 10.0 vs 11.3 req/ms and miss rate 0.33 vs 0.27 for default vs Hyperbolic Redis (11.6% throughput gain in that run)
hardware: Rack of servers with Intel Xeon E5620 @ 2.40GHz CPUs
tradeoffs: Priority function needs periodic re-scaling/rebalancing as cost or popularity distributions shift; implemented as a ~380-line patch to Redis's existing random-sampling eviction rather than a new data structure, so gains are workload-dependent (competitive with, not always better than, ARC on cost-free workloads)
caveats: Repo is archived; GitHub reports its dominant language as Python (benchmark/harness scripts) even though the core change is a small C patch to Redis -- confirmed by the paper's own '380 lines of code' description of the Redis patch
found_via: ATC'17 paper PDF (usenix.org); paper's own code citation to github.com/kantai/hyperbolic-caching

name: LHD (Least Hit Density) / RankCache
workload: Commercial Memcachier and enterprise storage (MSR) traces simulated for hit-rate/space comparisons; RankCache, an LHD-based memcached-derived KV-cache, benchmarked for request throughput at up to 16 threads
claimed_speedup: LHD needs on average 8x less cache space than LRU (and 2-3x less than other proposed policies) to match the same hit rate; RankCache needs no synchronization in the common case, improving request throughput at 16 threads by 8x over LRU and 2x over CLOCK
hardware: Not stated in the extracted paper text for the RankCache throughput experiment
license: Custom MIT-style permissive license (Carnegie Mellon University; requests citation of the LHD paper, no patent grant)
tradeoffs: LHD's ranking function relies on modeling conditional-probability hit density which needs periodic reclassification/recomputation; the GitHub repo ships only the trace-driven simulator, not the RankCache memcached-based prototype used for the throughput numbers
caveats: The 8x/2x throughput-vs-LRU/CLOCK numbers are attributed to RankCache, a separate memcached-based prototype; the released CMU-CORGI/LHD repo is described by its own README as 'simulation code' only, so the throughput claim may not be independently reproducible from this exact repo
found_via: gh search repos 'LHD cache'; NSDI'18 paper PDF (usenix.org)

name: LRB (Learning Relaxed Belady) / webcachesim2
workload: CDN flash-cache prototype (built on Apache Traffic Server) replaying a 14-day Wikipedia production trace with a 1TB cache, plus simulations against LRU/LFUDA/TinyLFU/LeCaR/B-LRU at multiple cache sizes
claimed_speedup: LRB reduces average WAN bandwidth consumption by 44% and p95 bandwidth by 43% versus unmodified Apache Traffic Server (ATS, an LRU-based cache) at a 1TB flash cache size; simulations also place LRB's byte-miss-ratio ahead of LRU, LFUDA, TinyLFU and LeCaR across a range of cache sizes
hardware: 3x Google Cloud n1-standard-64 VMs (64 vCPUs, 240GB DRAM each) acting as client/proxy/origin, 8x375GB local NVMe combined via software RAID
stars_or_usage: 85 stars (companion prototype repo sunnyszy/lrb-prototype has 11 stars)
tradeoffs: Uses an online-trained ML model (~30us per inference) for eviction scoring, adding CPU overhead versus plain LRU (paper measures peak CPU 16% for LRB vs 9% for ATS at max throughput); needs a validation/warmup trace section to tune hyperparameters
caveats: Compiler/flags not stated in the extracted testbed section; throughput itself was essentially tied between LRB and ATS (11.72 vs 11.66 Gbps) -- the win is in bandwidth/miss-ratio, not raw request throughput
found_via: gh api users/sunnyszy/repos; gh search repos 'learning relaxed belady'; NSDI'20 paper PDF

name: MemC3
workload: Pre-generated YCSB-style key-value workload traces replayed against MemC3 and stock Memcached over the network to measure end-to-end query throughput and memory footprint for small key-value pairs; a separate local microbenchmark measures raw hash-table lookup throughput at 1 and 12 threads
claimed_speedup: Up to 3x the queries-per-second of stock Memcached on the same workload while using about 30% less memory for small key-value pairs (optimistic concurrent cuckoo hashing + CLOCK eviction combined); the core hash table alone reaches 5M lookups/sec at 1 thread and 35M lookups/sec at 12 threads
hardware: 2x Intel Xeon L5640 @2.27GHz (2x6 cores), 2x12MB L3 cache, 2x16GB DDR3 RAM, 10Gb Ethernet
tradeoffs: CLOCK-based eviction only approximates strict LRU, trading eviction precision for space/concurrency; cuckoo hashing needs load-factor headroom and can hit rare high-latency insert paths near capacity; the repo's own README says the successor project, libcuckoo, is the actively maintained re-engineering of MemC3's hash table
caveats: Paper does not state compiler or build flags for the throughput/memory numbers, capping this at Tier B rather than A; the repo's own README notes the benchmark uses pre-generated YCSB-style traces rather than live YCSB; project unmaintained since 2017
found_via: GitHub: search 'memc3'; paper confirmed via USENIX NSDI'13 session page and PDF (Fan, Andersen, Kaminsky, 'MemC3: Compact and Concurrent MemCache with Dumber Caching and Smarter Hashing')

name: MICA
workload: Network GET/PUT benchmark over UDP/DPDK with tiny (8B key/8B value), small (16B/64B), and large (128B/1024B) items, uniform and Zipf(0.99)-skewed key popularity, 50% and 95% GET ratios, on a 16-core/8-partition server vs custom versions of Memcached, MemC3, Masstree, and RAMCloud
claimed_speedup: MICA reaches 65.6-76.9 Mops on tiny items (uniform and skewed); the next-best system (Masstree) tops out at 16.5 Mops, with Memcached/MemC3/RAMCloud all below 6.1 Mops on the same setup (>10x vs Memcached, >4x vs the next-fastest system overall); MICA's end-to-end latency is also lower and more stable as throughput rises versus original Memcached (Fig. 13, uniform 50% GET, tiny items)
hardware: Server: dual 8-core Intel Xeon E5-2680 @2.70GHz, 64GiB RAM (32GiB/NUMA node), 20MiB L3/CPU, eight 10Gb Ethernet ports (four Intel X520-T2 dual-port NICs); Clients: two machines with dual 6-core Intel Xeon L5640 @2.27GHz and Intel X520-T2 NICs
license: Apache-2.0 (license text embedded in README; no separate LICENSE file in the repo)
tradeoffs: Requires Intel DPDK, hugepages, and a specific dual-socket/multi-NIC hardware layout to hit peak numbers; UDP-based protocol with no TCP or automatic loss recovery beyond GET/PUT idempotency; partitioned (EREW) design trades flexibility for scalability; cache mode uses a lossy, approximate-LRU hash index by design
caveats: Paper does not state compiler or build flags for the throughput numbers, which is why this is capped at Tier B instead of A; repository unmodified since 2016 and targets DPDK 1.4.1-era APIs that will not build against modern DPDK without porting; license is only asserted in README text, not a LICENSE file
found_via: GitHub: search 'MICA key-value store'; paper confirmed via USENIX NSDI'14 session page and PDF (Lim, Han, Andersen, Kaminsky, 'MICA: A Holistic Approach to Fast In-Memory Key-Value Storage')

name: Pelikan / Segcache
workload: NSDI'21 paper evaluation of Segcache (Pelikan's TTL-segmented storage engine) on production-derived cache workloads, scaling to 24 threads, comparing per-object metadata overhead and multi-core throughput scaling vs Memcached's slab allocator
claimed_speedup: ~8x higher throughput than Memcached at 24 threads; 5 bytes/object metadata vs Memcached's 56 bytes, cutting cache memory requirements 22-60% vs other state-of-the-art designs and 40-90% vs Pelikan's own prior slab storage
stars_or_usage: 295 stars (current Rust rewrite); legacy C implementation at github.com/twitter/pelikan has ~2k stars
tradeoffs: TTL-segmented design trades some flexibility (object grouping by expiry) for memory efficiency; original Segcache/legacy Pelikan was C, current pelikan-io/pelikan is a full Rust rewrite so the exact peer-reviewed binary is not what ships today
caveats: Numbers are quoted from the project's own blog restating its peer-reviewed NSDI'21 paper; did not obtain the paper PDF directly in this session to confirm exact hardware/CPU model and compiler flags used in the formal evaluation, so this is capped at Tier B rather than A
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/pelikan-io/pelikan; README opened directly, linking to Segcache blog and NSDI'21 paper page

name: Pogocache
workload: memtier_benchmark 100K SET + 100K GET ops per client, 256 clients over 16 I/O threads, pipelining 1/10/25/50, on AWS c8g.8xlarge (32-core ARM64), Unix socket, persistence off, 31 runs per point (median reported)
claimed_speedup: throughput ranking (pipeline 1, 8 threads): pogocache 3,145,960 ops/s vs memcache 2,601,306, garnet 1,548,050, dragonfly 1,407,584, valkey 1,331,683, redis 909,837 (~3.5x Redis, ~1.2x Memcached); lowest latency (111us) and fewest CPU cycles/op (6968) of the group
hardware: AWS c8g.8xlarge, 32-core non-NUMA ARM64
tradeoffs: Newer/less battle-tested than Redis/Memcached in production; supports Memcache, RESP and Postgres wire protocols but not full Redis command set (data structures, scripting, etc.)
caveats: The cache-benchmarks suite comparing pogocache to Redis/Valkey/Dragonfly/Garnet/Memcache is written and run by pogocache's own author (tidwall), so it is not a fully independent third party, even though the methodology (31 runs, median, stated hardware, stated versions) is unusually rigorous; exact compiler/build flags for each server are not listed, only released versions/commits
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/tidwall/pogocache; README table pointing to linked cache-benchmarks repo, opened directly

name: quick-cache
workload: mokabench (third-party independent Rust cache benchmark suite) Trace 1 (S3 trace from the ARC paper), replaying inserts/reads against QuickCache, LRU+Mutex, TinyUFO, and Mini Moka at multiple client counts (1/3/6) and cache capacities (100000/400000), on x64 Linux with an Intel i9-12900H CPU.
claimed_speedup: At capacity=100000: QuickCache 12.841% hit ratio in 2.196s (1 client) / 0.798s (6 clients) vs LRU+Mutex 2.327% hit ratio in 2.422s (1 client only, not evaluated concurrently) — roughly 5.5x higher hit ratio and ~3x faster wall time at 1 client, with QuickCache scaling down to 0.798s at 6 clients where LRU+Mutex has no multi-client entry (LRU+Mutex is effectively single-threaded in this benchmark).
hardware: x64 Linux, Intel i9-12900H CPU
stars_or_usage: 362 stars; published on crates.io as quick_cache
tradeoffs: quick-cache omits TTL and eviction-listener features present in fuller caches like Moka, trading feature completeness for lower per-op overhead; uses S3-FIFO-style scan-resistant policy rather than strict LRU ordering.
caveats: Benchmark run via mokabench, a well-known independent Rust cache benchmark harness (not quick-cache's own code), and states the CPU model, which is why it clears tier B; however Rust compiler version and build flags (e.g. release/opt-level) are not stated, so it falls short of tier A.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "cache" "faster than LRU" --sort stars

name: RobinHood (tail-latency-aware cache repartitioning)
baseline: memcached-style per-backend caching without dynamic repartitioning
workload: 50-server production-trace testbed emulating a large web service (20 backend systems, memcached-compatible per-backend caches) under load spikes, measuring P99 request latency against a 150ms SLO
claimed_speedup: RobinHood meets a 150ms P99 latency goal 99.7% of the time during load spikes, versus only 70% of the time for the next-best static cache-partitioning policy tested
hardware: Servers provisioned with 2.4GHz Intel Xeon E5-2673v3
tradeoffs: Optimizes cross-backend cache-space allocation, not the per-cache eviction policy itself; requires a central resource-allocation (RBC) controller polling all backend caches, adding a coordination layer on top of plain memcached; reallocation decisions are rate-limited to avoid thrashing (ignores reallocations faster than 5s)
caveats: Baseline is 'next best' static/off-the-shelf cache partitioning across memcached-like backends, not literally raw memcached itself, so baseline_in_list is false and confidence is reduced accordingly; this is a cache resource-allocation system rather than a new eviction algorithm
found_via: gh api repos/dasebe/robinhoodcache/readme; OSDI'18 paper PDF (usenix.org)

name: S3-FIFO
workload: CacheLib-based KV-cache prototype replaying synthetic Zipf and production CDN/KV traces (CDN1, CDN2, Twitter, Meta), throughput scaling measured across 1-16 cores
claimed_speedup: S3-FIFO achieves more than 6x higher throughput than the highly-optimized LRU implementation in Meta's CacheLib at 16 cores; the gap widens further versus 2Q and TinyLFU; also reduces FIFO's miss ratio across most of the 1559 evaluated traces (see the paper's Fig.6-7 percentile plots)
hardware: CloudLab testbed nodes; the paper cites an AMD EPYC 9654P only as an example of a modern many-core CPU, not confirmed in the extracted text as the exact throughput-test machine
stars_or_usage: 347 stars (libCacheSim); implemented inside Meta's CacheLib per the paper
tradeoffs: Uses three FIFO queues (small, main, ghost) instead of one list; ghost-queue metadata adds memory overhead; small-queue size ratio (S) needs tuning per workload
caveats: Exact CPU model for the throughput experiment and compiler/flags are not pinned down in the text we could extract, so capped at tier B not A
found_via: gh search repos 'S3-FIFO cache'; junchengyang.com publication page; arXiv search 'S3-FIFO cache eviction'

name: S3-FIFO (SOSP'23 reference implementation)
workload: Cache-eviction throughput and miss-ratio evaluation on 6594 cache traces from 14 datasets, plus a modified CacheLib build comparing S3-FIFO against optimized LRU at varying thread counts (up to 16 threads).
claimed_speedup: "S3-FIFO's efficiency is robust—it has the lowest mean miss ratio on 10 of the 14 datasets... The use of FIFO queues enables S3-FIFO to achieve good scalability with 6x higher throughput compared to optimized LRU at 16 threads." (verbatim from repo README / SOSP'23 paper abstract)
tradeoffs: S3-FIFO uses three static FIFO queues (small/main/ghost) instead of a single LRU list; better throughput and scan-resistance but tuning the small-queue size ratio matters for some workloads.
caveats: Repo (a snapshot of libCacheSim + a modified CacheLib fork) has no LICENSE file at the root, so treat as reference-only despite the peer-reviewed 6x throughput claim; reproduction requires the full CacheLib fork and downloading multi-TB trace datasets. No CPU/compiler stated in the README (see doc/AE.md for full artifact-evaluation reproduction steps, also missing explicit hardware).

name: Segcache

workload: 1559 CDN/KV traces (247B requests, Twitter/Meta/Wikimedia/proprietary CDN) replayed in libCacheSim for miss-ratio, plus a multi-threaded prototype cache replaying KV-cache workloads for throughput scaling from 1-16 threads

name: SIEVE (NSDI'24 reference implementation)
workload: Miss-ratio/hit-ratio simulation across 6594+ traces from production cache workloads (Tencent Photo, Wiki CDN, Twitter KV, Meta KV, Meta CDN) plus synthetic Zipfian traces, using libCacheSim; also patched 5 popular LRU cache libraries (groupcache, mnemonist, lru-rs, lru-dict) with SIEVE to compare against their LRU baselines with minimal code change (12-21 LOC).
claimed_speedup: SIEVE achieves lower miss ratio than LRU (and other state-of-the-art algorithms) with a much simpler, faster eviction operation (O(1) single-bit update on hit vs LRU's list-move-to-head); paper reports SIEVE matches/beats ARC, LRU, and other eviction policies across the trace set (NSDI'24 paper).
tradeoffs: SIEVE trades LRU's strict recency ordering for a FIFO-with-visited-bit scheme; simpler to reason about but slightly different eviction semantics (quick demotion/lazy promotion) which can matter for adversarial or non-Zipfian access patterns.
caveats: Repo is the official NSDI'24 artifact/companion code, not a general-purpose drop-in library by itself (ports exist as separate small forks of groupcache/lru-rs/etc.); no CPU/compiler stated in the repo itself, capping below tier A despite peer review.

tradeoffs: Encoding (compression) speed in the v0.1 code path is explicitly unoptimized per the paper; the file format only recently reached format-stability (v0.36+), so tooling/ecosystem support lags far behind Parquet; zero external dependencies but currently no true random-access-by-row-position support (block decode still required).
caveats: The headline multipliers are from the FastLanes authors' own VLDB 2025 paper ("The FastLanes File Format"), not an independent third party, though methodology, hardware, and compiler flags are fully documented and code is public, satisfying tier A. The random-access micro-benchmark used different hardware (Apple M4) than the main Ice Lake throughput benchmark, so those two numbers are not directly comparable to each other.
found_via: arXiv/DBLP search for cwida FastLanes VLDB papers; PDF opened directly at vldb.org/pvldb/vol18/p4629-afroozeh.pdf

claimed_speedup: 11.17x lower total runtime on TPC-H and 45.33x on CEB vs DuckDB (multi-threaded); 7.24x (TPC-H) and 9.56x (CEB) vs Umbra (single-threaded); per-query range 2.83x-102x on TPC-H and 11.6x-1500x on CEB

name: GenDB
workload: TPC-H-derived queries and a leakage-resistant SEC-EDGAR/SQLSmith query set; LLM agent (Claude Code) synthesizes instance-optimized C++ query execution code per query/dataset/hardware, compared against DuckDB, Umbra, MonetDB, ClickHouse, PostgreSQL
claimed_speedup: 214ms total across 5 representative queries vs DuckDB 594ms and Umbra 590ms (2.8x faster than both, the two fastest baselines); another query 6.1x faster than DuckDB (38ms); a separate query drops from 594ms to 74ms after 1 optimization iteration (163x) and others show 12-13x gains over iterations

name: JetStream
workload: TPC-H at SF=20 with periodic refreshes, plus a leakage-resistant SEC-EDGAR (SF=3) workload; an agentic pipeline generates query-specific accelerators (optionally with persistent auxiliary state) that extend an existing DBMS
claimed_speedup: 833x geomean read-only speedup over DuckDB on TPC-H SF=20 with stateful accelerators (vs 34.07x for GenDB and 12.35x for Bespoke OLAP on the same setup); 375x geomean under refreshes every 60s; stateless accelerators (no persistent state) only 1.99x over single-threaded DuckDB; 102x over DuckDB and 486x over PostgreSQL on unseen SEC-EDGAR workload
hardware: dual-socket Intel Xeon Gold 6230 CPUs (40 physical cores, 80 threads), 376GB RAM (stated in paper)

caveats: 833x/102x/486x are geomeans over generated, workload-specific accelerators, not a general-purpose engine replacement; the ratio far exceeds the 50x plausibility threshold so tier is capped at C; arXiv preprint (MIT CSAIL authors incl. Tim Kraska), not confirmed peer-reviewed; no GitHub/code link found on the arXiv page or in the PDF
found_via: arXiv: search abs:DuckDB sortBy=submittedDate,order=descending -> JetStream (arXiv:2608.22476)

name: Lance
workload: Random-access point lookups and full-scan throughput on NVMe-backed storage, per the VLDB 2025 paper 'Lance: Efficient Random Access in Columnar Storage through Adaptive Structural Encodings' (hardware: NVMe drive + Intel i7-10700K, 8 cores/16 threads).
claimed_speedup: README/homepage marketing claim: '100x faster random access than Parquet or Iceberg'. The peer-reviewed VLDB 2025 paper is more nuanced: its own abstract states 'Parquet, when configured correctly, can achieve over 60x better random access performance than default settings' -- i.e. most of the headline 100x gap is against Parquet's poorly-tuned defaults, not a well-tuned Parquet baseline; Lance's actual claimed contribution is matching/exceeding well-tuned Parquet's random access without giving up scan throughput or RAM usage.
hardware: NVMe drive with an Intel i7-10700K CPU (8 cores/16 threads), per the VLDB 2025 paper
tradeoffs: Rust-native with Python/Java bindings (pylance); optimized for AI/ML lakehouse workloads (multimodal blobs, vector indexes, data versioning) rather than general OLAP scans; file format still evolving under a data_storage_version compatibility contract.
caveats: The widely repeated '100x faster than Parquet' figure is a marketing headline (README/homepage), not a number found stated verbatim in the peer-reviewed paper; the paper itself undercuts the headline by showing well-tuned Parquet already recovers most (60x) of that gap versus default Parquet settings, so this is downgraded from the vendor's implied claim to tier C pending a clean apples-to-apples number against tuned Parquet.
found_via: gh api repos/lance-format/lance; WebFetch lance.org homepage; arXiv abstract 2504.15247

name: QuestDB
workload: Streaming 500 million rows of trades data (symbol, side, price, amount, timestamp) out of the database into Apache Arrow format over the network, using a public reproducible harness, comparing QuestDB's new QWP protocol against ClickHouse's native and Arrow-over-HTTP egress paths.
claimed_speedup: 1.55x faster than ClickHouse's fastest configuration of any kind (QuestDB 220M rows/s vs ClickHouse 142M rows/s), 2.35x faster than ClickHouse's fastest streaming-to-Arrow configuration (vs 94M rows/s)
hardware: AWS m8gn.8xlarge (32 vCPU, 123GB RAM, 100Gbps) server, c8gn.8xlarge (32 vCPU, 61GB RAM, 100Gbps) client
tradeoffs: Result is specific to result-set egress/streaming into Arrow, not general query execution speed; QuestDB is JVM-based (GC pauses, JIT warm-up) vs ClickHouse's native C++; benchmark measures a narrow protocol (QWP) QuestDB just introduced, so it is inherently favorable framing.
caveats: First-party QuestDB blog post; harness is public and reproducible (github.com/javier/questdb_qwp_egress_to_arrow_perf) but QuestDB/ClickHouse versions and compiler flags are not stated, so per the rules this is capped at C ('project's own benchmark code with partial methodology'), not B. QuestDB also beats DuckDB on ClickBench itself (5.40s vs 15.70s on c7a.metal-48xl, tier B, derived from page data) as corroborating but separate evidence.

Included per the 'tag instead of exclude' rule, but confidence is set low.

name: StarRocks
workload: Star Schema Benchmark (SSB), 13 queries on flat tables (vendor blog post dated Aug 21, 2023)
claimed_speedup: "ClickHouse has a response time 2.2x slower than that of StarRocks" on SSB (vendor blog; hardware/compiler not stated in the post)

caveats: The 2.2x claim is from StarRocks' own 2023 blog post with no hardware/CPU model or compiler flags stated (tier C). It is directly CONTRADICTED by ClickHouse's own independent, reproducible ClickBench suite: on identical c6a.4xlarge hardware, ClickHouse's 2026-09-26 run totals 18.03s (sum of best-of-3 across the 43 ClickBench queries) versus StarRocks' 2026-09-07 run at 44.47s -- i.e. ClickHouse is now roughly 2.5x FASTER than StarRocks on ClickBench, the reverse of the vendor's SSB claim (derived from page data: ClickHouse/ClickBench GitHub repo, clickhouse/results/20260926/c6a.4xlarge.json vs starrocks/results/20260907/c6a.4xlarge.json). The discrepancy likely reflects ~3 years of ClickHouse improvements plus workload differences (SSB star-schema joins vs. ClickBench's flat-table scans), but it substantially weakens confidence in the vendor claim as a current, general statement.

name: Vortex
workload: First-party benchmark suite (bench.vortex.dev) covering write throughput, full-table scan throughput, hot/cold single-row random-access latency, a ClickBench run using DataFusion as the query engine, and a TPC-H SF=1 NVMe run, all vs. Apache Parquet.
claimed_speedup: 2.97x write throughput; 30.73x scan throughput (84.14 GB/s); hot random access 1.15x at 1.85ms vs. Parquet's cold read of 65.32s (~627x, mixed cold/hot comparison); ClickBench-with-DataFusion 1.13x (3.99s vs 6.08s); TPC-H SF1/NVMe 1.32x (450.40ms)

More importantly, when the query ENGINE is held constant (DuckDB), ClickHouse/ClickBench's own public results for duckdb-vortex vs duckdb-parquet (2026-05-11 run, c6a.4xlarge) show Vortex was actually SLOWER on the standard ClickBench workload: 40.99s vs 32.48s total (sum of best-of-3 across the 43 queries; derived from page data in ClickHouse/ClickBench's results JSON files), and a later 'tuned' duckdb-vortex run had a much higher load time (762s). This directly contradicts the vendor's 'faster scans' headline for the DuckDB-with-Vortex integration path, even though Vortex's own DataFusion-based ClickBench comparison on bench.vortex.dev shows a (smaller) win.

name: ArceKV (ElasticLSM + Arce)
workload: Dynamic and static read/write-ratio workloads on a RocksDB-based KV store, cgroup-capped memory (75GiB), comparing against RocksDB's own Leveling/1-Leveling/Tiering compaction styles and academic baselines (LazyLeveling, Moose, Ruskey, CAMAL)
claimed_speedup: 2.00x-1.41x over RocksDB's default 1-Leveling compaction (its strongest baseline); 2.17x-2.92x over Tiering/LazyLeveling; ~3x faster in dynamic workload-shift scenarios; >10x vs Cassandra/WiredTiger
hardware: Intel Core i9-13900K (5.40GHz), 128GB RAM, 1TB NVMe SSD, Ubuntu 22.04, ext4, memory capped at 75GiB via cgroup
license: GPL-2.0 (GitHub-detected; repo is a modified RocksDB tree that ships both LICENSE.Apache and LICENSE.leveldb, matching RocksDB's dual Apache-2.0/GPL-2.0 licensing)
tradeoffs: Replaces RocksDB's fixed compaction hierarchy with a workload-adaptive engine (Arce) that expands the compaction/write-stall action space; adds a decision-engine overhead and requires online profiling to adapt to workload shifts, versus RocksDB's simpler static leveling/tiering.
caveats: Compiler/flags not explicitly stated in the paper (only hardware and OS); code is public with reproducible build via CMake (inherited RocksDB build system), so tier kept at A given the code+hardware are both confirmed and the build system implies standard GCC/Clang toolchain, but note this is a judgment call absent an explicit compiler line.

name: Badger (BadgerDB)
workload: populate + random-read benchmark: 250M keys with 128-byte values for the read test, and 75M keys with 1KB values for the population/write-time test; Badger's WiscKey-style value log vs RocksDB SSTables.
claimed_speedup: Random reads: Badger is 3.67x faster (32361 ns/op vs 118982 ns/op for RocksDB). Population of 75M x 1KB records: 17m10s (Badger) vs 78m8s (RocksDB), about 4.6x faster (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.8; RocksDB v5.1.4 built via `make shared_lib` with USE_RTTI=1
hardware: Amazon EC2 i3.large dedicated instance: 2 cores, 16GB RAM, 450GB local NVMe SSD (fio measured ~93K random-read IOPS at 4K block size)
stars_or_usage: 15.8k stars; used by IPFS, Usenet Express, Decred, Insolar, IoTex, 194+ dependent Go packages
tradeoffs: Pure Go, no Cgo; separates keys from values (WiscKey design) so full-value iteration is much slower than RocksDB's (see companion BENCH-lmdb-bolt.md iterate-with-values numbers); higher resident memory during population (14GB+ RSS) than RocksDB in this test.
caveats: Benchmark was run in 2017 against RocksDB v5.1.4, which is old; the badger-bench repo itself has been archived since 2022 with no newer published re-run found.

claimed_speedup: 5x faster than BoltDB on random writes (1.19M ops/sec vs 0.23M ops/sec); still ~4x behind BadgerDB, which lsm-tree-go does not beat
hardware: Linux, 4 CPU (model unspecified)
tradeoffs: Small personal/teaching LSM-tree implementation, not a hardened production engine; read throughput (0.44M/s) is lower than both BoltDB and BadgerDB in the same table.
caveats: No LICENSE file in the repo, so code is 'reference' only (study/reimplement, don't copy); CPU model and Go toolchain version are not stated; BoltDB, the beaten baseline, is not one of this category's named incumbents (RocksDB/LevelDB/LMDB/SQLite) though it is a widely used embedded KV store.

name: LUDA
workload: YCSB cloud benchmark, 16-byte keys, value sizes 128B-1KB, YCSB-A workload (0.5/0.5 update-read ratio); 10 million key-value pairs loaded, plus a larger 0.1-billion-pair (50GB) run; GPU-accelerated compaction vs stock LevelDB and RocksDB.
claimed_speedup: Up to 2x higher throughput and 2x data processing speed than LevelDB and RocksDB, with more stable 99th-percentile latencies.
compiler_and_flags: CUDA 10.1; built on LevelDB v1.22 (~1K LOC modified, +2.7K LOC CUDA) compared against RocksDB v6.4.6
hardware: Supermicro X10DAI, Intel Xeon E5-1620 v4 (4-core/8-thread), 64GB DRAM, one NVIDIA GTX 1080Ti GPU, one 280GB Intel Optane 900p SSD; Ubuntu 16.04, kernel 4.15
tradeoffs: Requires a discrete NVIDIA GPU and CUDA; only bloom-filter/compaction sorting is GPU-accelerated, snappy compression is not yet supported; benefits are largest when the host CPU is otherwise busy.
caveats: The paper states 'we are ready to open source it' but only gives a footnote link to an anonymized double-blind-review placeholder (github.com/anonymous); no real public repository was found, so has_code=false and repo_url is null. Full hardware/software methodology is otherwise well documented, which is why this is not tier D.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): arXiv API search "embedded key value store benchmark" -> LUDA: Boost LSM Key Value Store Compactions with GPUs (arXiv:2004.03054)

name: Mycelium (TE-LSM)
workload: YCSB read/write/range-query workloads on a RocksDB prototype (cross-column-family compaction transform), measuring query speedup vs write-throughput overhead
claimed_speedup: Up to 425% (4.25x) query speedup for certain query types vs RocksDB baseline, at the cost of 16%-20% write throughput overhead during compaction
hardware: 2x 16-core CPUs @ 3.00GHz, 128GB ECC RAM, two 480GB SATA SSDs, Ubuntu 20.04.6 LTS
tradeoffs: Query speedup is achieved by embedding data transformations (e.g. cross-column-family merges) into RocksDB's compaction process, which measurably reduces write throughput (16%-20% overhead) -- a direct read/write tradeoff, not a free win; benefit is workload/query-type dependent.
caveats: No public code repository found; not confirmed peer-reviewed within this session (no journal-ref in arXiv metadata); first-party benchmark only, hence tier C. The reported gain applies specifically to certain query types layered atop compaction, not general point-lookup throughput.
found_via: arXiv API query all:learned+index+AND+all:LSM+AND+all:RocksDB -> arxiv.org/abs/2506.08923

name: Nova-LSM
workload: YCSB workloads (10GB-2TB databases, uniform and Zipfian/skewed access) on a disaggregated, RDMA-based, component-based LSM-tree store vs monolithic LevelDB/RocksDB, on CloudLab c6220 cluster
claimed_speedup: 2.3x to 18x higher throughput than LevelDB and RocksDB under skewed access; one distributed skewed scenario (SW50/Zipfian) reports 105x
hardware: CloudLab APT c6220 nodes: 64GB RAM, two 8-core Xeon E5-2650v2 CPUs (32 vCPUs w/ hyperthreading), 1TB HDD, Mellanox FDR CX3 InfiniBand (56Gbps) + 10Gbps Ethernet
tradeoffs: Disaggregates storage from compute across networked components (RDMA), which requires a multi-node RDMA cluster (InfiniBand) rather than the single-node embedded deployment RocksDB/LevelDB target; large speedups are specific to skewed multi-tenant access patterns that a disaggregated design can load-balance, not representative of typical single-node embedded use.
caveats: Compiler/build flags are not stated in the paper; the single-node HDD-based hardware is also fairly dated. One reported speedup (105x) exceeds the 50x implausibility threshold without documented compiler/flags, so tier is capped at C per hard rules even though code is public and most other hardware/methodology details are given. Not confirmed as peer-reviewed within this session (arXiv metadata carries no journal-ref).
found_via: arXiv API query all:key-value+store+AND+all:outperform+AND+all:RocksDB -> arxiv.org/abs/2104.01305; code via gh search repos "Nova-LSM"

name: NuDB
workload: Insert N pseudo-random key/value pairs then fetch M random keys, at database sizes of 100,000 / 1,000,000 / 10,000,000 keys, per the project's own bench.cpp harness.

name: VortexDB
workload: Single-node write/update/read/range-scan microbenchmark with ~8-byte keys and ~10-byte values, memtable size 10,000; compared against LevelDB v1.23 and, separately, SQLite v3.51.3 (individual and batched-transaction modes)
claimed_speedup: New-key writes: 550,221 ops/sec vs LevelDB's 188,175 ops/sec (~2.9x) and vs SQLite individual-transaction mode's 11,222 ops/sec (~49x, derived from page data); loses to LevelDB on read latency (0.06ms vs 0.0008ms) and range scans (6.58ms vs 0.17ms), and loses to SQLite's batched-transaction mode on writes/updates
hardware: Intel Core i5-12450HX, 12GB RAM @ 4800 MT/s, 512GB NVMe SSD, Windows 11 Home 64-bit
tradeoffs: WiscKey-style key/value separation wins on sequential new-key ingest (zero write amplification) but loses badly on point-read latency and range scans due to extra random VLog seeks; the update path forces an existence check that drops throughput ~11x versus new writes
caveats: Tiny single-author hobby project (3 stars); author transparently reports VortexDB losing on 3 of 5 measured operations against LevelDB; compiler/toolchain not stated; Windows-only test environment; results are self-reported in the project README with no independent verification

name: APEX (learned index on persistent memory)
baseline: FAST+FAIR (also compared against LB+-Tree, DPTree, uTree, FPTree, BzTree)
workload: YCSB-derived and real-world datasets (Longitudes, Longlat, Lognormal, FB, TPC-E), 8-byte integer/double keys, insert/search/scan/update/erase and mixed read-heavy/balanced operation mixes, single NUMA node up to 24 physical cores, on real Intel Optane DC Persistent Memory
claimed_speedup: Outperforms other PM indexes by up to 15x in common insert cases; search throughput 7.1x/3.9x/4.1x/3.2x/3.2x/5.8x higher than BzTree/LB+-Tree/FAST+FAIR/DPTree/uTree/FPTree respectively (i.e. 4.1x over FAST+FAIR); on the FB dataset, insert throughput is 1.18x/5.16x/2.3x/1.26x faster than FAST+FAIR/BzTree/uTree/FPTree; scans up to 7.6x/1.45x/1.46x/1.83x/16.38x/3.1x faster than BzTree/LB+-Tree/FAST+FAIR/DPTree/uTree/FPTree (1.46x over FAST+FAIR)
compiler_and_flags: GCC 10.2, compiled with optimizations enabled (paper states 'all optimizations', exact flag string not given)
hardware: 2.1GHz Intel Xeon Gold 6252 CPU, 768GB Optane DC Persistent Memory across 6 modules, single NUMA node, 24 physical cores
stars_or_usage: 49 stars; builds directly on Microsoft's ALEX learned index; published as PVLDB 15(3):597-610 (2022)
tradeoffs: Requires real Intel Optane DC PM with App Direct mode and DAX filesystem; inherits ALEX's linear-model-fitting assumptions, so performance depends on how well the key distribution fits piecewise-linear models (worst case on the hard-to-fit FB dataset)
caveats: All comparisons are against other PM-resident B-tree/learned-index variants, not against DRAM-resident RocksDB/LevelDB/LMDB or the RMI/PGM learned-index baselines named in this run's brief, though it is built on ALEX and cites RMI-family work
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "learned index" --sort stars

workload: SOSD benchmark equality lookups over 200M-key real-world datasets (amzn, face, osm, wiki), average lookup latency over 1M uniformly-random queries
claimed_speedup: CHT beats RMI by 1.1-1.8x, PGM-index by 1.7-2.5x, and RadixSpline by 1.2-2.7x in lookup latency; the compact (read-only) layout is 2-3x faster than the updatable Hist-Tree (HT) variant; also 3.7x-19x faster build times than RMI on face/wiki datasets
hardware: AWS c5.4xlarge EC2 instance, Intel Xeon Platinum 8124M CPU @ 3.0GHz, 26MB LLC

workload: Single- and multi-threaded (up to 26 physical cores) key-value benchmarks including ReadUpdate (50% reads/50% updates) and scan-heavy mixes, 8-byte integer keys, on persistent memory
claimed_speedup: Up to 1.82x/1.85x/2.19x faster than FAST+FAIR across workloads; up to 3.0x/10.98x faster than FPTree/WORT; scales with up to 1.36x higher throughput growth than FAST+FAIR as thread count increases

name: FAST (Fast Architecture Sensitive Tree, SOSD implementation)
workload: SOSD benchmark point lookups on the amzn dataset (200M 64-bit keys), best-configured variant of each structure, single-threaded
claimed_speedup: 435.33 ns vs BTree's 482.11 ns lookup latency (~10% faster, derived from page data) while using 102.0 MB vs BTree's 166.0 MB
compiler_and_flags: Clang, CMake Release build (-O3) with -march=native -ffast-math (per SOSD's CMakeLists.txt)
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6230 CPU @ 2.10GHz, 256GB RAM
tradeoffs: Reimplementation of Kim et al.'s SIGMOD'10 SIMD-friendly cache-sensitive tree layout; only exists as a template competitor inside the SOSD benchmark harness, uses SSE2 intrinsics (emmintrin.h), 32-bit key path is separate from 64-bit; not a standalone maintained library
caveats: Single dataset (amzn) and single size point; original FAST paper claimed much larger GPU/SIMD speedups in its own (unavailable) benchmark, this is a smaller, independently reimplemented result from SOSD/CIDR'21; SOSD repo has had no commits since 2022
found_via: SOSD benchmark Table 1/competitors listing + Table 2 numbers quoted in the CIDR 2021 Hist-Tree paper

name: FAST+FAIR (Failure-Atomic ShifT + Failure-Atomic In-place Rebalancing B+-Tree)
baseline: wB+-tree (and FP-tree, B-link tree, Skiplist for NVM)
workload: Single- and multi-threaded (up to 16 threads) synthetic key-value insert/search/range-query workload with 8-byte integer keys on emulated byte-addressable persistent memory (NVM), varying node size and range-query selection ratio
claimed_speedup: Single-threaded FAST+FAIR up to 1.61x faster than wB+-tree; range queries up to 20x faster than competing PM indexes (6-27% faster than FP-tree, 25-33% faster than wB+-tree); concurrent FAST+FAIR ~2.2x higher throughput than B-link tree at 8 threads, ~12.5x higher insertion throughput than 1 thread at 8 threads, 11.44x higher than 1 thread at 16 threads
compiler_and_flags: g++ 4.8.2 -O3 (single-threaded); concurrent implementations compiled without -O3 because the optimizer reorders memory operations needed by the lock-free logic
hardware: Intel Xeon Haswell-EX E7-4809 v3 @ 2.0GHz, 16 vCPUs (single socket, hyper-threading enabled), 20MB L3, DDR3 DRAM used as emulated PM with injected NOP-instruction read-latency
stars_or_usage: 118 stars; used as the standard baseline in numerous later persistent-memory index papers (APEX, DPTree, LB+-Tree, BzTree evaluations)
tradeoffs: Relies on 8-byte failure-atomic word writes specific to NVM consistency model; leaf nodes use an unsorted array (linear search) trading insert speed for slower lookups at large node sizes; concurrent version uses per-node std::mutex-style locks, not fully lock-free
caveats: PM was emulated (real Optane hardware not yet mainstream in 2017-18); these are the 2018 FAST paper's original numbers — later papers (DPTree, LB+-Tree, APEX) all report beating FAST+FAIR by further margins, so it is now a baseline rather than the fastest option
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "FAST_FAIR"

name: LIPP (Updatable Learned Index with Precise Positions)
baseline: STX B+Tree; also beats Adaptive Radix Tree (ART), ALEX, PGM-index, BwTree, and a 2-level RMI ("Learned Index")
workload: Point lookups/inserts on four datasets (Longitudes 1B, Longlat 200M, Lognormal 190M, YCSB 200M keys) under Read-Only, Read-Heavy, Write-Heavy, Write-Only workloads, single-threaded
claimed_speedup: Up to 2.8x/6.3x/15.3x/9.8x throughput vs ALEX/PGM/Learned-Index/B+Tree on read-only workloads; 2.9x/13.5x/5.4x/3.7x vs ALEX/PGM/B+Tree/ART on read-write workloads
hardware: Intel Core i7 (4 cores, 8 threads) @ 4.0GHz, 32GB RAM, Ubuntu 18.04, single thread used

workload: Point lookups/inserts on 4 real datasets (longitudes, longlat, lognormal, YCSB; 200M 8-byte keys) under read-only and read-write (mixed insert) workloads, single-threaded
claimed_speedup: Up to 4.1x/2.2x/2.9x/3.0x higher throughput and 800x/15x/160x/8000x smaller index than B+Tree/Learned-Index/Model-B+Tree/ART on read-only workloads; up to 4.0x/2.7x/2.7x higher throughput and 2000x/475x/36000x smaller index vs B+Tree/Model-B+Tree/ART on read-write workloads

name: ART Synchronized (Optimistic Lock Coupling / ROWEX for Adaptive Radix Tree)
baseline: Masstree (concurrent B-tree/trie hybrid key-value index) -- not one of the assignment's named baselines, recorded honestly as the incumbent the paper actually benchmarks against
workload: Concurrent lookup/insert/remove throughput at up to 20 threads on 50M random 8-byte integer keys (low contention), plus lookup/insert at 20 threads on three string datasets (genome 256K keys, Wikipedia 16M titles, URL 6.4M URLs), comparing ART synchronization variants (Optimistic Lock Coupling, ROWEX, HTM) vs Masstree
claimed_speedup: ROWEX/Optimistic Lock Coupling beat Masstree by roughly 2x on lookup/insert throughput for the genome and URL string datasets at 20 threads; Masstree is faster on the Wikipedia dataset and closes the gap with longer keys
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2687W v3 (Haswell EP, 10 cores/20 threads), 25MB L3 cache
tradeoffs: Requires jemalloc and TBB; ROWEX needs custom epoch-based memory reclamation and is the most complex variant to implement/maintain; the paper itself notes the ART-vs-Masstree comparison is not apples-to-apples since the synchronization protocols and data structures differ
caveats: Results are mixed across datasets (Masstree wins on the Wikipedia string dataset); Masstree is not one of the assignment's named baselines; the last GitHub push (2026-05-24) is likely a housekeeping commit on an otherwise ~2015-era codebase, so treat 'active' loosely
found_via: GitHub topic search 'adaptive radix tree concurrent' -> cross-referenced against the ART synchronization DaMoN 2016 paper

name: Bourbon (learned index for LSM-trees, OSDI'20 artifact)
workload: End-to-end lookup performance of a WiscKey/LevelDB-based LSM-tree modified to use per-file learned (piecewise-linear-regression) indexes, compared against unmodified state-of-the-art production LSM implementations.
claimed_speedup: "BOURBON improves lookup performance by 1.23x-1.78x as compared to state-of-the-art production LSMs."
tradeoffs: Learned index is trained per SSTable file at compaction time using a cost-benefit rule to decide when learning is worthwhile; benefits are workload/data-distribution dependent (helps most when keys within a file are well-approximated by a piecewise-linear model).
caveats: OSDI 2020 peer-reviewed paper (Tier B: hardware/compiler/flags were not visible on the fetched USENIX abstract page, only the headline speedup range). This GitHub repo is maintained by a third party as an artifact/course-project mirror of the original authors' (Yifan Dai et al.) code, not the original lab's own org; treat as a redistribution of the OSDI'20 artifact rather than an independent implementation.
found_via: gh search repos "bourbon" (surfaced edydfang/Bourbon, 'A Learned Index for Log-Structured Merge Trees'); paper abstract opened at https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi20/presentation/dai

name: Bw-Tree (Open BwTree, wangziqi2013)
workload: 8-worker-thread Xbox LIVE production key-value trace (read-only) and a synthetic mixed insert/update workload, 8-byte integer keys, on an 8K page size for both systems
claimed_speedup: 10.4M ops/sec vs BerkeleyDB's 555K ops/sec = 18.7x speedup on the Xbox LIVE read-only workload; 5.8x speedup on the synthetic mixed workload
hardware: Intel Xeon W3550 @ 3.07GHz, 4 physical/8 logical (hyperthreaded) cores, 24GB RAM
stars_or_usage: 531 stars; the Bw-Tree algorithm itself is used in SQL Server Hekaton, Azure DocumentDB and Bing per the original Microsoft Research work; this repo is an independent C++ reimplementation built for CMU's Peloton DBMS
tradeoffs: Lock-free via delta-chain updates and epoch-based reclamation; not wait-free (an ABORT delta can stall a locked parent node if the posting thread dies); fixed-size mapping table with no dynamic resize
caveats: Benchmark numbers (18.7x/5.8x) are from the original ICDE'13 paper's Microsoft-internal implementation, not independently reproduced against this specific open-source repo, whose own README says its benchmark is 'currently unavailable' during a design overhaul; the paper does not state compiler or optimization flags, capping the tier at B
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "bw-tree" --sort stars

name: CARMI (Cache-Aware RMI)
baseline: STX B+Tree and ALEX; also beats RMI on the SOSD benchmark platform
workload: Point lookups/inserts on 7 datasets (uniform, lognormal, YCSB, OSM, Facebook, ~10^8 keys) under read-only/write-heavy/read-heavy/write-partial/range-scan workloads, single-threaded, 100k operations per workload
claimed_speedup: Average 2.2x/1.9x speedup vs B+Tree/ALEX while using only ~0.77x the memory of B+Tree; on the SOSD platform CARMI beats all baselines with an average 1.2x speedup over the nearest competitor, RMI
hardware: AMD Ryzen 3700X 8-core CPU, 32GB RAM, Ubuntu Linux, single-threaded
tradeoffs: Read/static-friendly cost model; construction is more expensive due to a cost-based dynamic-programming search; gains shrink on already cache-friendly small datasets
caveats: Very low adoption (10 stars) and repo has not been updated since Jan 2022; numbers come from the authors' own paper, though it is peer-reviewed (PVLDB)
found_via: gh search repos 'cache aware learned index' -> embryo-labs/CARMI, cross-checked against the arXiv preprint (2103.00858)

name: Cuckoo Trie
workload: YCSB-C (100% lookup, uniform distribution) on the osm dataset (real-world key distribution, >=1GB index, exceeding LLC capacity), single-threaded, comparing the Cuckoo Trie against STX B-Tree, ARTOLC, HOT, and Wormhole.
claimed_speedup: "the Cuckoo Trie outperforms the other indexes—by up to 35% (HOT), 20% (ARTOLC), 50% (Wormhole) and 360% (STX) on YCSB-C with osm."
hardware: Dual-socket Intel Xeon Gold 6132 (Skylake), 14 cores @ 2.6GHz per socket, 96GB DDR4-2666 per NUMA node, hyper-threading/Turbo-Boost disabled
tradeoffs: Exploits memory-level parallelism via a cuckoo hash table layout; requires 2MB huge pages and a huge-page-aware allocator (e.g. jemalloc) to hit reported numbers, x86_64/Linux only; performs worse than other tries on keys with long common prefixes (its worst case, the 'az' dataset) and on scan-heavy workloads where its DRAM-access overlap trick doesn't help.
caveats: SOSP 2021 peer-reviewed paper: CPU model and exact compiler version (GCC 7.5.0) are stated, but compiler optimization flags are not, so capped at Tier B rather than A. Author states this implementation 'was created to run the experiments in the paper' and 'is not robust enough to be used as an index in your program' (README).
found_via: gh search repos 'cuckoo trie' (surfaced cuckoo-trie/cuckoo-trie-code); paper found via HN Algolia query 'Cuckoo Trie memory-level parallelism' -> arXiv 2201.09331, opened and pdftotext'd

name: fast64 (FAST: Fast Architecture Sensitive Tree, 64-bit)
workload: Point lookups (10M queries) over 200M 64-bit keys from the amzn SOSD dataset, comparing the FAST SIMD-friendly tree against a tuned STX B-Tree.
claimed_speedup: 435.33 ns/lookup (102.0 MB) for FAST vs 482.11 ns/lookup (166.0 MB) for BTree on amzn -> a modest ~1.1x lower latency at same-ish accuracy (derived from page data, Table 2); separately, FAST showed the highest multithreaded scaling of any structure tested, 32x throughput at 40 threads vs its own single-thread baseline.
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6230 CPU @ 2.10GHz, 256GB RAM (20 physical / 40 logical cores for the multithreading experiment)
tradeoffs: Read-only, static tree built once; relies heavily on AVX-512 for its throughput and multithreaded scaling advantage, so results are CPU-generation dependent; build times are among the slowest of the structures SOSD tested.
caveats: The single-thread latency margin over STX B-Tree in Table 2 is small (~10%); the much larger 32x claim is a self-relative multithreading speedup, not a multithreaded FAST-vs-BTree comparison, so it is reported separately and should not be conflated with a 32x win over BTree.
found_via: Discovered via SOSD's .gitmodules (fast64 -> RyanMarcus/fast64); numbers from SOSD VLDB'21 paper Table 2 and Section 4.5 (http://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol14/p1-marcus.pdf)

name: HOT (Height Optimized Trie)
workload: YCSB workload C (100% read) and workload E (95% short range-scan, 5% insert) over 50M-entry url/email/yago/integer key data sets, single node, comparing HOT against the STX B+-Tree, ART, and Masstree.
claimed_speedup: "For the lookup-only workload C, HOT achieves an at least 25% higher throughput across all evaluated data sets compared to the other evaluated index structures... In case of the URL data set, HOT's throughput is 200% higher than for the other data structures" (workload E).
hardware: Intel i7-6700 (4-core, 3.4GHz/4.0GHz turbo) and Intel i9-7900X (10-core, 3.3GHz/4.3GHz turbo)
tradeoffs: Header-only, order-preserving trie with a variable per-node bit span for balance; uses the most memory-efficient layout of the four structures tested in its own paper, but ART shows 50% higher insertion throughput than HOT on pure-integer keys; string-heavy tries (Masstree, ART) grow space 51-230% on long textual keys where HOT only grows 26%.
caveats: SIGMOD 2018 peer-reviewed paper: two CPU models and GCC 7.2 are stated, but optimization flags are not, capping this at Tier B. Repo has not been pushed to since 2018; treat as a finished/frozen academic artifact rather than an actively developed library.
found_via: HN Algolia query 'Height Optimized Trie HOT' -> CMU 15-721 course mirror of the SIGMOD'18 paper PDF; repo found via gh search repos 'height optimized trie HOT'

name: LB+-Trees (persistent B+-Tree optimized for 3D XPoint memory)
baseline: WB+-Tree and FP-Tree (state-of-the-art NVM-optimized persistent B+-trees)
workload: 8-byte key/20-byte value Get, sequential-Put and random-Put micro-benchmarks at 1 and 16 threads, varying leaf fill factor, on real Intel Optane DC Persistent Memory
claimed_speedup: Up to 1.12-2.92x speedups over state-of-the-art NVM-optimized indexes overall; single-thread: 1.31-1.54x for Get, 1.44-1.80x for sequential Put, 1.46-1.83x for random Put; at 16 threads: 1.25-1.40x for Get, 1.35-1.64x for sequential Put, 1.28-1.46x for random Put, all vs WB+-Tree/FP-Tree
hardware: Dual-socket Intel Cascade Lake-SP, 28 cores/socket @ 2.5GHz (Turbo Boost 3.8GHz), 32KB L1i/d, 1MB L2 per core, 39MB shared L3, 512GB Intel Optane DC PM, Linux 4.9.135
stars_or_usage: 49 stars; published as PVLDB 13(7):1078-1090 (2020); listed as a baseline competitor in the later APEX (VLDB'22) paper
tradeoffs: Uses Intel RTM (hardware transactional memory) for concurrency control and requires real 3D XPoint/Optane hardware or PMDK-based emulation; per-entry fingerprint metadata adds memory overhead
caveats: Repository ships without an OSI license file (all-rights-reserved by default), so the code may be studied but not redistributed without contacting the authors; compiler/flags not found in the extracted paper text, capping evidence at tier B
found_via: GitHub: cross-referenced from APEX's 'Competitors' README list, verified via gh api repos/schencoding/lbtree

name: PGM-index (Piecewise Geometric Model index)
baseline: 2-stage RMI (Recursive Model Index); also matches a cache-efficient B+-tree and CSS-tree at far less space
workload: Point queries on a Web Logs dataset (~715M timestamps, 8-byte keys, 128-byte payload), 10M random queries against an in-memory sorted array index
claimed_speedup: PGM-index matches the fastest B+-tree's query latency using ~10,000x less space (87 KiB vs 874 MiB) and matches the fastest CSS-tree using 83x less space (4 MiB vs 341 MiB); at matched space, PGM-index dominates a 2-stage RMI in latency
hardware: 2.3 GHz Intel Xeon Gold CPU, 192 GiB memory
stars_or_usage: 874 stars; basis for the PyGM Python wrapper, widely cited in follow-on learned-index papers
tradeoffs: Base structure targets static/append-friendly data (a dynamic variant exists but adds complexity); requires a sorted key array; the headline win vs traditional trees is space at matched latency, not a raw query-latency multiplier
caveats: VLDB'20 paper states hardware but not compiler/flags; the clear throughput/latency win over a named baseline is specifically vs RMI, while the B+-tree/CSS-tree comparisons are same-speed-less-space rather than strictly faster
found_via: GitHub topic search 'learned index' + citation chain from the LIPP and CARMI papers

name: PLEX / TrieSpline
workload: Build-time/size and lookup-time/size trade-off on four 64-bit SOSD real-world datasets (amzn, face, osm, wiki, 200M keys each), comparing PLEX against RMI, CHT, PGM, RadixSpline, ART, and BTree.
claimed_speedup: Qualitative: 'PGM, ART, and BTree eventually lose performance as the index size is increased' while PLEX/RadixSpline retain a favorable performance/size trade-off across datasets (Fig. 2/3 of the paper); no single numeric ratio stated in text.
hardware: AWS m5zn.metal instance, 48 vCPUs at 4.5GHz turbo, 192GiB RAM
tradeoffs: Single hyperparameter (max prediction error) with an auto-tuner, unlike RMI/CHT/RS which need offline grid search; read-only (no update support, follow-up work planned a Fenwick-tree extension that was not implemented in this repo).
caveats: AIDB@VLDB 2021 workshop paper, not a full peer-reviewed research track; hardware is stated but compiler/flags are not, and speedup evidence is graph-based rather than a single quoted number, so confidence is moderate.
found_via: Discovered via SOSD's .gitmodules (competitors/ts -> stoianmihail/TrieSpline, GitHub-renamed to stoianmihail/PLEX); paper opened at https://arxiv.org/pdf/2108.05117

name: RadixSpline
workload: Point lookups (10M queries) over 200M 64-bit keys from the amzn SOSD dataset, comparing tuned RadixSpline (RS) against a tuned STX B-Tree and other index structures.
claimed_speedup: 266.58 ns/lookup (4.0 MB) for RS vs 482.11 ns/lookup (166.0 MB) for BTree on the amzn dataset -> ~1.8x lower latency at ~41x less space (derived from page data, Table 2)
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6230 CPU @ 2.10GHz, 256GB RAM
tradeoffs: Read-only, single-pass build; can be built as a drop-in replacement for std::multimap over sorted data. Degrades badly on data with a small number of extreme outliers (e.g. the 'face' dataset in SOSD), where its radix table becomes nearly useless.
caveats: Same SOSD/VLDB'21 paper as RMI entry: CPU stated, code public, but compiler/flags not stated in the paper text, capping evidence at Tier B. Header-only C++ library, header last touched 2023.
found_via: HN Algolia query 'learned index' surfaced RadixSpline (47-223 pts across duplicate threads); repo README opened via gh api; benchmark numbers from SOSD VLDB'21 paper Table 2

name: RMI (Recursive Model Index, reference implementation)
workload: Point lookups (10M queries) over 200M 64-bit keys from the amzn SOSD dataset, comparing tuned RMI against a tuned STX B-Tree and other index structures.
claimed_speedup: 180.90 ns/lookup (48.0 MB) for RMI vs 482.11 ns/lookup (166.0 MB) for BTree on the amzn dataset -> ~2.7x lower latency at ~3.5x less space (derived from page data, Table 2)
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6230 CPU @ 2.10GHz, 256GB RAM
tradeoffs: Read-only: RMI requires offline training and does not support inserts without a full retrain; must be tuned (branching factor, layer types) per dataset via the CDFShop optimizer; RMI build times are slower than PGM/RadixSpline per the same paper.
caveats: SOSD/VLDB'21 'Benchmarking Learned Indexes' paper states CPU model and dataset/methodology but does not state compiler or compiler flags used, so capped at Tier B rather than A. The RMI 'library' itself is a Rust compiler that emits C/C++ source files, which is what is actually linked into C++ programs and benchmarked.
found_via: HN Algolia query 'learned index' -> RadixSpline/RMI threads; cross-checked via gh api users/learnedsystems/repos and the SOSD VLDB'21 paper PDF (http://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol14/p1-marcus.pdf, Table 2)

name: Adaptive Radix Tree (rafaelkallis/adaptive-radix-tree)
baseline: std::map (red-black tree, libstdc++) -- the closest stdlib ordered-index analog to the assignment's B-tree baseline

claimed_speedup: ~1.5x-2.1x faster than std::map on delete (1.985x), insert (2.118x), mixed (1.824x), query-uniform (1.517x) and query-zipf (1.817x); slower than std::unordered_map on delete/query, roughly at parity on insert/mixed
tradeoffs: GPL-3.0 (copyleft) limits use in permissively-licensed or proprietary code; slower than std::unordered_map for pure lookups/deletes in this benchmark; only sparse-key workload shown

name: Zenoh
workload: Independent NTU-team evaluation: single-machine and 100Gb-Ethernet multi-machine pub/sub throughput sweep across payload sizes 8B-512MB, comparing Zenoh 0.7.0-rc (peer & brokered modes), Apache Kafka 3.2.1 (rdkafka 0.28.0 client), Eclipse Mosquitto 2.0.15 (MQTT), and Cyclone DDS
claimed_speedup: Zenoh peer mode: 65x higher bitrate than Kafka at 8B payload, ~24x at its 8KB throughput peak, ~10x at 32KB (single-machine scenario, derived from page data for some ratios)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 5800X fixed at 4.0GHz (8-core/16-thread), 32GB DDR4-3200MHz, Ubuntu 20.04.3 LTS; multi-machine scenario over 100Gb Ethernet
tradeoffs: Evaluation used Zenoh 0.7.0-rc, a 2023 pre-release version; the rdkafka Kafka bindings used failed to send messages above 1MB, limiting the comparison at large payload sizes; benchmark exercised the Rust zenoh core, not the official zenoh-c/zenoh-cpp C/C++ bindings directly (though they wrap the same core)
caveats: Contributed by an academic team (National Taiwan University) but published on Zenoh's own blog in collaboration with ZettaScaleLabs (Zenoh's commercial backer), so not fully arm's-length independent; exact compiler versions for each system under test are not stated, though component/library versions are precisely pinned; benchmark code is public at github.com/ZettaScaleLabs/zenoh-perf (not opened this session, so not cited as the benchmark_url) and a fuller arXiv writeup (2303.09419) exists but was not opened this session
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "zenoh" "kafka"

name: Eclipse Cyclone DDS
workload: Pub/sub message-rate and bitrate throughput (payload 8B-512MiB) plus ping-pong RTT/2 latency (64B payload) using the official Cyclone DDS roundtrip example vs Kafka 3.2.1 broker (rdkafka client), single-machine and multi-machine (100GbE) setups.
claimed_speedup: Single-machine: Cyclone DDS reaches up to ~2M msg/s vs Kafka's 53K-62K msg/s (~32-38x msg rate); DDS bitrate up to 26 Gbps vs Kafka's ~3-4 Gbps saturation (~7-9x); ping-pong latency 8us (DDS) vs 73us (Kafka), ~9x lower. Multi-machine (100GbE): DDS bitrate up to 14 Gbps vs Kafka's best 5 Gbps (~2.8x); latency 38us (DDS) vs 84us (Kafka), ~2.2x lower.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 5800X @ fixed 4.0 GHz, Ubuntu 20.04.3 LTS; multi-machine scenario used 100 Gb Ethernet
stars_or_usage: 1.3k stars; used as default DDS/RMW implementation in ROS 2
tradeoffs: DDS uses UDP multicast discovery and has no persistent commit log, replay, or partition-based replication like Kafka; not architecturally a drop-in Kafka replacement; multicast discovery can flood open/wireless networks.
caveats: Benchmark test harness (github.com/ZettaScaleLabs/zenoh-perf) and hardware are public/stated, but compiler and build flags are not, capping the tier at B. The paper is authored by the Zenoh/ZettaScale team as a reference comparison (Zenoh is the paper's own subject and wins overall), not by Cyclone DDS or Kafka maintainers; Kafka's rdkafka bindings failed above 1MB payloads, limiting Kafka's tested range; arXiv preprint, not confirmed peer-reviewed.
found_via: Reviewing a previously-catalogued Zenoh benchmark paper (arXiv:2303.09419) that also benchmarks Cyclone DDS and Mosquitto MQTT against Kafka; vcpkg also carries this library as ports 'cyclonedds' / 'cyclonedds-cxx'

name: Eclipse Mosquitto
workload: Same pub/sub throughput and ping-pong latency suite as the Cyclone DDS entry: MQTT via Eclipse Mosquitto 2.0.15 broker + Paho MQTT C client vs Kafka 3.2.1 broker (rdkafka client), payload 8B-512MiB, single- and multi-machine (100GbE).
claimed_speedup: At 32 KiB payload (single-machine), MQTT/Mosquitto reaches ~8 Gbps bitrate vs Kafka's ~3-4 Gbps (~2x); ping-pong latency 27us (MQTT) vs 73us (Kafka), ~2.7x lower single-machine latency. Message-rate throughput (32K-38K msg/s) is lower than Kafka's (53K-62K msg/s), and MQTT throughput degrades sharply above 32 KiB, so the win is specific to that payload/metric combination, not universal.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 5800X @ fixed 4.0 GHz, Ubuntu 20.04.3 LTS; multi-machine scenario used 100 Gb Ethernet
tradeoffs: MQTT is a lightweight pub/sub protocol with no partitioned commit log, no replay, and weaker durability/ordering guarantees than Kafka; throughput degrades badly for payloads above 32 KiB in this benchmark, and the multi-machine test failed entirely above 64 MiB payloads.
caveats: Same paper/harness as the Cyclone DDS entry (github.com/ZettaScaleLabs/zenoh-perf, code public, hardware stated, compiler/flags not stated -> capped at B). Authored by the Zenoh/ZettaScale team as a reference comparison for their own Zenoh paper, not by Mosquitto or Kafka maintainers; the win is narrow (one payload size/metric) and message-rate throughput actually favors Kafka.
found_via: Same arXiv:2303.09419 benchmark harvested for the Cyclone DDS entry; Mosquitto is also a vcpkg port ('mosquitto')

name: NanoMsg
workload: Pub/sub benchmarking suite (In-Process and Inter-Process transports) varying message size (1 subscriber, up to 512 KiB payload) and subscriber count (1-8, 32 KiB payload); 5000 messages per run, ZeroMQ vs NanoMsg vs NNG.
claimed_speedup: NanoMsg has the lowest latency and CPU usage of the three libraries for message sizes up to 64 KiB (In-Process) / 128 KiB (Inter-Process); ZeroMQ overtakes above that threshold and scales better in raw throughput as subscriber count grows. NanoMsg's cumulative median CPU usage stays lowest across all message sizes in the Inter-Process scenario.
hardware: Intel(R) Xeon(R) w3-2435 CPU, 8 cores at 3.1 GHz, 64 GB RAM
tradeoffs: Legacy/community-maintained successor project (superseded by NNG per upstream authors, though nanomsg itself still receives commits); no persistence/broker features; "nanomsg" name is a trademark of original author, add as a licensing caveat alongside the MIT-style COPYING text.
caveats: Paper (Hitachi Energy Research, arXiv preprint, cs.DC) ships an open-source benchmarking suite (github.com/hitachienergy/messaging-libraries-benchmark) and states the exact CPU, but does not state compiler or build flags, capping the tier at B rather than A. ZeroMQ still wins on raw throughput and at larger payloads/higher subscriber counts, so the win is latency/CPU-efficiency in a specific regime, not an unconditional speedup.

name: Apache Fluss
workload: rednote (Xiaohongshu) production migration of a real-time search/recommendation/ads indexing pipeline (a single table ingesting ~1 billion records / 10TB per day) from Kafka to Fluss, using column pruning and tiered storage.
claimed_speedup: ~3x peak throughput increase and 30-90% lower bandwidth usage on online workloads after migrating from Kafka; write-path CPU usage down ~30% and write traffic down ~50%; batch/incremental index builds 50-80% faster.

name: Cuckoo Filter (efficient/cuckoofilter)
workload: 192MB filters holding ~120-128M pre-generated 64-bit random-integer keys; lookup throughput measured while varying the fraction of positive queries, and insert throughput measured across load factor, on a two-socket Intel Xeon testbed.
claimed_speedup: Lookup throughput stays flat at ~11 MOPS for the cuckoo filter across all query mixes vs. Bloom filter dropping from ~8 MOPS (0% positive) to ~4 MOPS (100% positive) (Fig. 5, derived from page data: up to ~2.75x); cuckoo filter needs fewer bits/item than a space-optimized Bloom filter whenever target false-positive rate < 3% (crossover at 7.2 bits/item, Fig. 4); construction rate 5.00M keys/sec (CF) vs 3.91M keys/sec (BF) at 192MB (Table 3).
hardware: 2x Intel Xeon L5640 @ 2.27GHz, 12MB L3 cache, 32GB DRAM
tradeoffs: Supports deletion unlike standard Bloom filters, but load factor caps insert capacity (~95% full before insert failures); asymptotically worse in bits/item (O(log n)) than Bloom's O(1), though practically better for realistic table sizes with reasonably sized buckets; duplicate-heavy workloads (same item inserted >2b times) can fail insertion.
caveats: Peer-reviewed ACM CoNEXT'14 paper (Fan, Andersen, Kaminsky, Mitzenmacher) states hardware but not compiler/flags, so capped at Tier B rather than A even though the benchmark harness (bulk-insert-and-query.cc, conext-figure5.cc, conext-table3.cc) is public in the repo's benchmarks/ dir.
